column3: It directly reverses the focus's final clause: God-given guidance cannot be overturned by a misleader.
It explicitly commands reliance on God because He is sufficient as guardian.
It directly contrasts fear manufactured by Satan's allies with fear of God alone.
It repeats both that none can protect from God and that one whom God misguides has no guide.
Its guidance and misguidance are borne by each person, complementing the focus's warning about lost direction.
It shows fabricated supports vanishing from those who have lost themselves.
It denies helpers apart from God and states that God-misguided people have no way out.
It answers an attempted intimidation with God's sufficiency and His guardianship.
Divine reinforcement is presented as sufficient help, though in a specific battle setting.
It joins refusal of God's call, lack of protectors apart from Him, and manifest misguidance.
The immediately following ayah tests alleged rivals' inability to remove harm or withhold mercy, then declares God sufficient.
It sets guidance and manifest error against acknowledged divine provision, but does not state the focus's protection claim.
It explicitly says that those whom God misguides will find no protectors apart from Him.
God's sufficiency for believers is shown by averting battle, though without the focus's guidance or fear themes.
Its contrast in worship only faintly bears on the focus's identity of God's servant.
It contrasts God's standing custody over every soul with false partners and repeats that the God-misguided have no guide.
The punishment of Satan's followers does not clarify sufficiency, false protection, or divine guidance.
It directly pairs God's firming of believers with His misguidance of wrongdoers.
It names the Quran as God's guidance and repeats that one whom God misguides has no guide.
The command to continue acting does not materially illuminate the focus's claims.
It explicitly assigns guidance to God.
The rhetorical affirmation of God's judgment shares a form of divine adequacy but not the focus's themes.
It directly declares that God is sufficient for the Prophet and the believers who follow him.
It presents divine warning as fear directed toward servants, unlike the illegitimate intimidation in the focus.
It denies any protector apart from God when His decree of harm comes.
The prospect of punishment does not explain the focus's sufficiency or guidance claim.
Exclusive worship of God and warning of judgment support the focus's rejection of rival reliance.
It warns those who will meet their Lord that they have neither protector nor intercessor apart from Him.
It explicitly says God is sufficient when deception is feared and names His support.
It challenges alleged beings apart from God to show any creative share, undermining their claimed power.
God's superior knowledge of the grateful does not materially clarify the focus.
All intercession and the dominion of heaven and earth belong to God, supporting the denial of independent intermediaries.
The mention of two additional gardens has no meaningful connection to the focus.
It affirms God's knowledge of all that people invoke apart from Him, but does not specify their impotence.
God's servants lie outside Satan's authority, and the Lord is sufficient as guardian.
A social accusation that believers are astray does not illuminate divine guidance or protection.
It names Zechariah as God's servant but adds no claim about sufficiency or guidance.
It immediately questions taking intercessors apart from God when they own nothing and lack understanding.
It concisely portrays God finding and guiding one who was lost.
Revelation to God's servant only loosely relates to the focus's servant and guidance language.
God's sufficient knowledge and sight of servants' sins supports His comprehensive guardianship.
Signs are sent as warning, which only broadly relates to the focus's theme of fear.
God sends clear signs to His servant to bring people from darkness into light.
It declares God creator of everything and guardian over everything, grounding His sufficiency.
Turning from false powers to God supplies the positive counterpart to refusing dependence on rivals.
The straight Book revealed to God's servant has a limited relation to divine guidance.
God explicitly undertakes to suffice the Prophet against the mockers.
It concerns God rendering the deeds of those who bar His path lost, not the focus's exact guidance claim.
The condemnation of lying about God does not clarify the focus's operative themes.
God's possession of the keys of heaven and earth supports His exclusive effective control.
It joins God's measured ordering with His guidance, though without the focus's protection context.
Divine power to revive the dead is not a close explanation of the focus.
It denies the Prophet a guardianship role over others, only indirectly delimiting human protection.
The brothers' charge that their father is in error is unrelated to the focus's divine guidance claim.
The Furqan is sent to God's servant as warning, with only a limited link to the focus.
God's control of provision supports sovereignty broadly but not the focus's specific claims.
It explicitly describes exchanging guidance for misguidance and losing direction.
The absence of fear for the blessed is only a broad contrast to the focus's intimidation theme.
It pairs guidance and misguidance with personal consequence, complementing the focus's warning about lost direction.
The brothers' mistaken charge of old error does not clarify divine misguidance.
It distinguishes warning from the continuing availability of a guide for every people.
God's uniqueness and overpowering authority support the focus's rejection of rivals.
God's justice toward servants only indirectly frames the focus's servant language.
God's testimony is sufficient to settle denial, though the sufficiency is evidentiary rather than protective.
God's taking and releasing souls in sleep and death demonstrates the effective control behind His sufficiency.
Solomon is called an excellent servant, without addressing protection or guidance.
Mockers receiving the consequence of their mockery does not materially illuminate the focus.
It commands reliance on God when entering peace, supporting reliance on Him as sufficient.
It presents God as the one who guides through darkness and rejects associating rivals with Him.
The recurring fate of mockers does not clarify sufficiency, fear, or guidance.
It commands reliance on the Ever-Living and says He is sufficient in knowledge of His servants.
It names manifest misguidance in a context of worshiping others, but does not state divine control of guidance.
Divine knowledge of those most deserving of the Fire does not clarify the focus.
The Creator and sovereign over the heavens and earth is presented as the reliable one to consult.
Sincere servants are excluded from Satan's reach, supporting the focus's contrast between God's servant and hostile intimidation.
God's sufficiency as knower does not closely address the focus's guardianship or guidance.
God is sufficient as witness because He fully knows and sees His servants.
It denies that the Prophet is astray, but does not explain God's guidance or the lack of a guide.
Hostile reaction to recited signs loosely resembles the intimidation surrounding the focus.
The self's sufficiency for final accounting is a distinct use of sufficiency.
God is explicitly sufficient as both guide and helper amid prophetic hostility.
Exclusive worship of God and fear of punishment support the focus's rejection of alternative objects of fear.
It declares God's sole dominion over life and death and denies any protector or helper apart from Him.
It promises that God will guide those who strive for Him along His ways.
God is sufficient as witness concerning worship, supporting His sole authority in a dispute over devotion.
It says no guardian can secure revelation against God's will, an indirect parallel to exclusive dependence.
It questions what army could help people apart from the Merciful, exposing false security.
God's servants are told not to fear, broadly contrasting the focus's imposed fear.
In threatened disaster, it warns that no guardian may be found, reinforcing the limits of protection.
The phrase that Hell is sufficient concerns punishment, not God's sufficiency as guardian.
Failure through corrupting the self does not clarify the focus's themes.
It calls invoking nonresponsive beings apart from God the deepest misguidance.
Those denying God's signs are turned away, a broad counterpart to misguidance.
It denies any shelter from God or refuge apart from Him.
God's demonstrated power over death broadly supports divine sovereignty but not the focus's specific claims.
Satan's claim over a share of God's servants helps frame the hostile pressure opposed by divine custody.
God's self-sufficiency and ownership of all in heaven and earth undermine false claims made about Him.
It distinguishes personal misguidance from guidance received through the Lord's revelation.
The image of scorching shade does not illuminate the focus.
It reduces invoked beings apart from God to fellow servants unable to answer, refuting their protective power.
It states that whomever God guides is rightly guided, while one He misguides finds no protecting guide.
It says that one whom God misguides has no protector after Him and no path of return.
It denies guidance to one whom God leaves astray and denies them helpers.
It distinguishes human desire to guide from God's exclusive knowledge and act of guiding.
It explicitly says that God misguides and guides whom He wills.
It declares that none can remove harm God causes except Him, directly grounding His sufficiency.
It likewise denies any remover of God's harm and any withholder of His mercy.
It explicitly declares that whoever relies on God, He is sufficient for that person.
It names God as believers' protector and the best of helpers.
It calls God the believers' protecting master and the best helper.
It grounds confidence amid threat in God as believers' protecting master.
It says God knows enemies best and is sufficient as protector and helper.
It denies anyone a protector or helper apart from God.
It challenges the taking of protectors apart from God who cannot benefit or harm themselves.
It affirms that God has no partner in His rule and shares judgment with none.
It exposes calling on one whose harm is nearer than benefit as choosing an evil protector and companion.
It denies any protector or helper apart from God.
It asks who can protect anyone from God if He wills harm or mercy.
It rejects taking gods apart from God because their intercession cannot avail and they cannot save.
It records and rejects treating others as protectors apart from God to obtain nearness through them.
It shows alleged gods apart from God failing to help when needed.
It identifies God as the protector of believers and denies that disbelievers have a protector.
